cor-shr-js-regression.title: James–Stein for regression
cor-shr-js-regression.html: Assume the normal linear model with X of full column rank p≥3, let SSE have m degrees of freedom (so SSE/σ2∼χ2(m), independent of 𝛃β^), and for c>0 let 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃β~c=(1−cSSEβ^⊤X⊤Xβ^)β^. Then, with 𝛃Z=(X⊤X)1/2β^, 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃E[(β~c−β)⊤X⊤X(β~c−β)]=pσ2−cm{2(p−2)−c(m+2)}σ4E‖Z‖−2. So 𝛃β~c dominates least squares in this loss iff 0<c<2(p−2)/(m+2), and the best constant is c=(p−2)/(m+2). In terms of the F statistic 𝛃𝛃F=(β^⊤X⊤Xβ^/p)/(SSE/m) for the hypothesis 𝛃β=0, the shrinkage factor is 1−cm/(pF).

def-shr-lasso.title: The lasso
def-shr-lasso.html:
For λ≥0, a lasso estimate 𝛃β^λL minimizes Lλ(b)=12‖y−Xb‖2+λ‖b‖1,‖b‖1=∑j|bj|.{#eq-shr-lasso}

This is the penalized form; the constrained form minimizes ‖y−Xb‖2 subject to ‖b‖1≤t. A vector s is a subgradient of ‖⋅‖1 at b, written s∈∂‖b‖1, if sj=sign(bj) when bj≠0 and sj∈[−1,1] when bj=0. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions for @eq-shr-lasso are X⊤(y−Xb)=λsfor some s∈∂‖b‖1;{#eq-shr-kkt}

that is, |xj⊤(y−Xb)|≤λ for every j, with xj⊤(y−Xb)=λsign(bj) whenever bj≠0.

def-shr-mse.title: Mean squared error
def-shr-mse.html: Let 𝛉θ~ be an estimator of 𝛉θ∈Rq with finite second moments. Its mean squared error matrix is 𝛉𝛉𝛉𝛉𝛉MSE(θ~)=E[(θ~−θ)(θ~−θ)⊤], its bias is 𝛅𝛉𝛉δ=E(θ~)−θ, and its total mean squared error is 𝛉𝛉𝛉trMSE(θ~)=E‖θ~−θ‖2. For estimators 𝛉𝛉θ~1,θ~2 we say that 𝛉θ~1 is at least as good in the matrix sense if 𝛉𝛉MSE(θ~2)−MSE(θ~1) is nonnegative definite.

def-shr-pcr.title: Principal component regression
def-shr-pcr.html: The principal components of the regressors are the vectors zj=Xvj=djuj, j=1,…,p. Their sample variances are dj2/(n−1), they are mutually orthogonal, and vj is the jth loading vector. For 0≤k≤p, the principal component regression estimate with k components is 𝛃𝛃β^kPC=∑j≤kα^jvj=VkVk⊤β^,Vk=[v1,…,vk], obtained by regressing y on z1,…,zk and transforming the coefficients back.

def-shr-ridge.title: Ridge regression
def-shr-ridge.html:
For λ≥0, a ridge estimate 𝛃β^λR minimizes ‖y−Xb‖2+λ‖b‖2.{#eq-shr-ridge-criterion}

The constant λ is the ridge parameter (or tuning parameter). The ridge trace is the curve 𝛃λ↦β^λR.

eq-shr-canonical.html: 𝛂𝛃𝛂𝛃α=V⊤β,α^=V⊤β^=D−1U⊤Y,cj=uj⊤Y=djα^j.

eq-shr-js.html: 𝛉𝛉E‖θ^JS−θ‖2=pσ2−(p−2)2σ4E‖Z‖−2<pσ2.

eq-shr-kkt.html: X⊤(y−Xb)=λsfor some s∈∂‖b‖1;

eq-shr-lasso.html: Lλ(b)=12‖y−Xb‖2+λ‖b‖1,‖b‖1=∑j|bj|.

eq-shr-ridge-criterion.html: ‖y−Xb‖2+λ‖b‖2.

eq-shr-ridge-mse.html: 𝛃𝛃E‖β^λR−β‖2=σ2∑jdj2(dj2+λ)2+λ2∑jαj2(dj2+λ)2.

eq-shr-stein.html: 𝛉E[(Z−θ)⊤g(Z)]=σ2E∑i=1p∂gi∂zi(Z).

exm-shr-js-risk.title: The risk function for ten means
exm-shr-js-risk.title_html: The risk function for ten means
exm-shr-js-risk.html: For p=10 and σ=1, the exact risk from @thm-shr-james-stein(b) is 2 at 𝛉θ=0, 4.784 at 𝛉‖θ‖2=5, 7.587 at 20 and 9.257 at 80, always below the constant risk 10 of Z (Figure 27.5.1). The fixed shrinkage Z/(1+0.5), which is ridge regression with λ=0.5 in an orthonormal design, has risk 𝛉(p+0.25‖θ‖2)/2.25 (@exr-shr-orthonormal-ridge). It beats James–Stein only on a middle range, 𝛉5.9<‖θ‖2<36.6. At the origin it is worse (10/2.25=4.44 against 2), it exceeds p once 𝛉‖θ‖2>5p=50, and it grows without bound. The dotted curve is the risk 𝛉𝛉p‖θ‖2/(p+‖θ‖2) of the best linear shrinkage fZ for each 𝛉θ, the oracle of @prp-shr-canonical(c) with a common factor; James–Stein stays within 2 of it without knowing 𝛉θ.

exm-shr-lasso-simulation.title: Three coefficient patterns
exm-shr-lasso-simulation.html:
Fix a design with n=50 and p=10, its rows drawn once from a normal distribution with correlations 0.5|j−k|, and columns scaled to ‖xj‖2=n; the errors are normal with σ=2. The coefficients are sparse, (3,−2,1.5,0,…,0); dense, ten coefficients ±0.5 with alternating signs; or intermediate, five coefficients ±1 and five zeros. Each method’s tuning constant (λ, or the subset size, with the best subsets found among all 1024) minimizes the error on an independent copy of the responses, an idealized validation set. The table gives the average of 𝛃𝛃‖Xβ~−Xβ‖2/(pσ2) over 300 data sets; least squares has expectation one (@exr-shr-smoother-mse), and the Monte Carlo standard error of each entry is about 0.02.

Pattern least squares ridge lasso best subset
sparse 1.02 0.95 0.74 0.46
dense 0.99 0.73 0.83 1.03
intermediate 0.99 0.84 0.86 0.90

Best subset selection is far ahead in the sparse case and worst in the dense case, where it cannot shrink and finds no zeros; ridge is the reverse; the lasso is never best and never worst. In the intermediate case the paired difference between the lasso and ridge is 0.02 with a standard error of 0.01. Hastie, Tibshirani and Tibshirani (2020) reached similar conclusions in a much larger study, adding that the ranking depends strongly on the signal-to-noise ratio (Figure 27.4.2 displays the table).

exm-shr-longley-js.title: James–Stein for Longley’s regression
exm-shr-longley-js.html: For Longley’s six slopes there are m=9 residual degrees of freedom and the overall F statistic is 330.3. The James–Stein factor with c=(p−2)/(m+2) is 0.99835: the regression fits far too well for shrinkage towards zero to help. The script therefore also simulates responses at Longley’s design with the least squares estimates divided by 60 as the truth, a weak signal whose noncentrality 𝛃𝛃β⊤X⊤Xβ/σ2 is about 0.6, with σ equal to Longley’s s. Over 20000 simulated data sets the ratio of the James–Stein prediction risk to that of least squares is 0.501.

exm-shr-longley-lasso.title: The lasso for Longley’s data
exm-shr-longley-lasso.html:
For the standardized Longley data, λmax=51813, and the variables enter in the order GNP, UNEMP, ARMED, YEAR, POP; the GNP deflator has not entered by λmax/1000. Figure 27.4.1(b) shows the path against the ratio of 𝛃‖β^λL‖1 to the ℓ1 norm of least squares. GNP, the regressor most correlated with employment, grows to over 3000; when YEAR enters, the two compete for the same direction, and GNP falls back to exactly zero and leaves the active set. Coordinate descent needs 42 sweeps at λmax/2, 157 at λmax/50 and 3479 at λmax/1000 for a tolerance of 10−10: the zigzag effect of collinearity.

Leave-one-out cross-validation, refitting the path without each year in turn, chooses λ=130, about 0.0025λmax, with 3 nonzero coefficients: −1303 for unemployment, −484 for the armed forces and 4475 for the year. Its minimized root mean squared error is 373, but as with ridge the minimum is optimistic; nested leave-one-out gives 428, level with least squares (425). What the lasso offers here is a simpler fit of equal accuracy, not a better one, and its choice of YEAR over GNP is exactly the kind that collinearity makes fragile.

The script checks the solutions at five values of λ three ways: the KKT conditions hold to within 10−6λ; a brute-force search over all 36=729 active sets and signs, solving the equations of @prp-shr-lasso-path, finds the same solution; and a bound-constrained optimizer on the split b=u−v, u,v≥0, finds no smaller criterion value.

exm-shr-longley-pcr.title: Principal components of Longley’s regressors
exm-shr-longley-pcr.html:
The six standardized Longley regressors have principal components whose shares of the total variance are 76.723%, 19.589%, 3.390%, 0.249%, 0.043% and 0.006%, so the usual rules of thumb keep two or three. The component t statistics are 42.66, 5.40, 10.66, −0.55, 3.96 and 1.72 (Figure 27.3.1(a)). The fifth component, with less than a two-thousandth of the variance, is nearly as strongly related to employment as the second, while the fourth, with more variance than the fifth and sixth together, is irrelevant.

Because principal component regression fits a projection (@prp-shr-pcr(a)), the leave-one-out prediction errors follow from @thm-res-deletion with the leverages 1/n+∑j≤kuij2. The root mean squared leave-one-out errors for k=0,1,…,6 are 3627, 1109, 1067, 506, 606, 435 and 425, in thousands. Adding the fourth component makes predictions worse, and adding the fifth makes them much better; the best number of leading components is 6, which is least squares itself. The rule tj2>2 keeps components 1,2,3,5,6. Applied once to all sixteen years and then treated as fixed, it gives 392, but that figure ignores the selection. Redoing the selection within each fold (nested leave-one-out) gives 444, worse than least squares. Searching all 64 subsets of components picks 1,2,3,5 with 389, optimistic for the same reason. With three leading components the coefficients are 1023, 1260, −1085, −417, 1070 and 966: all six regressors are retained, with the GNP and YEAR coefficients now positive and comparable.

exm-shr-longley-ridge.title: Ridge regression for Longley’s data
exm-shr-longley-ridge.html:
Longley’s regression (@exm-dep-longley) relates total employment, in thousands, to six economic series over n=16 years. With the regressors standardized, the eigenvalues dj2 of X⊤X run from 69.05 down to 0.0057. The least squares coefficients, in thousands of persons per standard deviation, are 163 for the GNP deflator, −3560 for GNP, −1888 for unemployment, −719 for the armed forces, −355 for population and 8709 for the year. The GNP and YEAR coefficients are large and of opposite sign: the two series rose together, and the data can hardly separate them.

Figure 27.2.1(a) shows the ridge trace against the effective degrees of freedom. As λ grows, the GNP and YEAR coefficients approach each other, and the GNP coefficient changes sign at λ=0.0110, where df=5.1. Leave-one-out cross-validation chooses λ=0.0026, with df=5.61, and GCV chooses λ=0.0030, with df=5.56. Both prefer little shrinkage. At the leave-one-out choice the coefficients are −6, −1809, −1645, −669, −825 and 7415. The largest changes are in the coefficients of GNP, YEAR and population, the three series that rose together, and the deflator coefficient is essentially zero. The minimized root mean squared leave-one-out error is 402, against 425 for least squares, but this minimum is optimistic, since the same errors chose λ. Choosing λ afresh within each leave-one-out fold (nested cross-validation) gives an honest 441: on these sixteen years tuned ridge does not predict better than least squares.

Panel (b) asks what the theorem guarantees in a world where the truth is the least squares fit, 𝛃𝛃β=β^, with σ=s=304.9. There, least squares has total mean squared error 19.33 million, and the best ridge estimate, at λ=0.0019 with df=5.69, has 15.01 million, a ratio of 0.777. @thm-shr-ridge-dominates(a) guarantees an improvement only for λ<0.00383, and part (c) gives dominance in the matrix sense for λ≤0.00200; in fact the improvement continues up to λ=0.0058. The ranges are narrow because this “truth” inherits the least squares estimate’s large components along the weak directions.

exm-shr-two-regressors.title: Two nearly collinear regressors
exm-shr-two-regressors.html:
Take n=50 observations of two centred regressors, scaled so that X⊤X=nR where R is a correlation matrix with off-diagonal entry 0.95. Let σ=1 and 𝛃β=(1,0.5)⊤. The eigenvalues of X⊤X are d12=n(1+0.95)=97.5 and d22=n(1−0.95)=2.5, with eigenvectors (1,1)⊤/2 and (1,−1)⊤/2. The canonical coefficients have sizes |α1|=1.0607 and |α2|=0.3536, and the signal-to-noise ratios are τ12=109.7 and τ22=0.3125. The first direction, the sum of the two regressors, is estimated precisely. The second, their difference, is not.

Estimator Factors (f1,f2) Total MSE
least squares (1,1) 0.4103
drop the second direction (1,0) 0.1353
halve the second direction (1,0.5) 0.1415
oracle fj∗ (0.991,0.238) 0.1054

Dropping the difference direction cuts the total mean squared error by two thirds, because τ22<1, and wins in the matrix sense too. Here ΔA=σ2v2v2⊤/d22 is singular, the bias is 𝛅δ=−α2v2∈C(ΔA), and 𝛅𝛅δ⊤ΔA+δ=α22d22/σ2=τ22=0.3125≤1. So by @thm-shr-bias-variance(c), every linear combination 𝛃a⊤β is estimated at least as accurately. Had the truth been 𝛃β=(1,−0.5)⊤, with the same length but pointing along the difference, then τ22=2.5×1.125=2.81 and dropping would have increased the total error.

exr-shr-augmented.title: A1
exr-shr-augmented.html: Show that 𝛃β^λR is the least squares estimate for the augmented data y~=(y⊤,0⊤)⊤ and X~=(X⊤,λI)⊤. Show that κ(X~)2=(d12+λ)/(dp2+λ), so ridge can be computed stably by QR (Chapter 10), and that the augmented problem has “residual sum of squares” 𝛃𝛃‖y−Xβ^λR‖2+λ‖β^λR‖2.

exr-shr-bias-length.title: B3
exr-shr-bias-length.html: Show that 𝛃𝛃E‖β^‖2=‖β‖2+σ2∑jdj−2. For which c does 𝛃cβ^ have smaller total mean squared error than 𝛃β^? Express the answer through 𝛃‖β‖2 and σ2tr(X⊤X)−1.

exr-shr-component-t.title: B1
exr-shr-component-t.html: Under the normal linear model with rank(X)=p<n−1 (centred data), show that the cj=uj⊤Y are independent N(djαj,σ2), independent of the residual sum of squares, and that tj=cj/s has a noncentral t distribution with n−p−1 degrees of freedom and noncentrality τj. Show that cj2/σ2−1 is unbiased for τj2.

exr-shr-coordinate-risk.title: B2
exr-shr-coordinate-risk.html: Let p be large and 𝛉θ=(pσ,0,…,0)⊤. Using the approximation 𝛉‖Z‖2≈‖θ‖2+pσ2, show that the James–Stein estimate of θ1 has mean squared error of roughly pσ2/4, far above the σ2 of Z1. Why does this not contradict @thm-shr-james-stein?

exr-shr-df-covariance.title: C1
exr-shr-df-covariance.html: For any estimator 𝛍μ^=SY of 𝛍μ=E(Y) with Cov(Y)=σ2I, show that σ−2∑iCov(μ^i,Yi)=trS. Deduce that df(λ) measures how strongly the ridge fit follows its own data, and that 𝛍E‖Y−HλY‖2=E‖HλY−μ‖2+nσ2−2σ2df(λ).

exr-shr-duplicate.title: B1
exr-shr-duplicate.html: Suppose x1=x2 and let b^ be a lasso solution with b^1+b^2=γ≠0. Show that every b with b1+b2=γ, b1,b2 of the sign of γ, and the other coordinates as in b^, is also a solution, whereas ridge regression gives b1=b2.

exr-shr-eb-ratio.title: B3
exr-shr-eb-ratio.html: In @prp-shr-empirical-bayes, show that the ratio of the Bayes risk of James–Stein to that of the Bayes rule is 1+2σ2/(pω2). When is the cost of estimating ω2 negligible?

exr-shr-generalized-ridge.title: B2
exr-shr-generalized-ridge.html: Generalized ridge regression uses a separate constant for each principal direction: 𝛃β^k=(X⊤X+VKV⊤)−1X⊤y with K=diag(k1,…,kp), kj≥0. Show that its shrinkage factors are dj2/(dj2+kj), and that the choice kj=σ2/αj2 gives the oracle factors of @prp-shr-canonical(c).

exr-shr-hidden-component.title: B2
exr-shr-hidden-component.html: Let x1,x2 be standardized regressors with correlation ρ=0.99 and let E(Y)=x1−x2. Find the canonical coefficients and show that α1=0. Compute τ12 and τ22 with n=100, unit-variance columns and σ=1. Which principal component regression is best, and what does a one-component principal component regression estimate?

exr-shr-inverse-moment.title: A1
exr-shr-inverse-moment.html: Show that E{1/χ2(m)}=1/(m−2) for m≥3 and that the expectation is infinite for m≤2. Deduce that the risk of the James–Stein estimator at 𝛉θ=0 is 2σ2 for every p≥3, however large p is.

exr-shr-js-subspace.title: C1
exr-shr-js-subspace.html: Let P be the orthogonal projection onto a fixed q-dimensional subspace of Rp, with p−q≥3. Show that PZ+(1−(p−q−2)σ2/‖(I−P)Z‖2)(I−P)Z dominates Z, and translate this into shrinking a regression fit towards a nested reduced model using its F statistic.

exr-shr-js-target.title: B1
exr-shr-js-target.html: 1. Show that for a fixed 𝛉θ0, the estimator 𝛉𝛉𝛉θ0+(1−(p−2)σ2/‖Z−θ0‖2)(Z−θ0) has risk 𝛉pσ2−(p−2)2σ4E‖Z−θ0‖−2. (b) Lindley’s estimator shrinks towards the grand mean: θ^i=Z¯+(1−(p−3)σ2/S)(Zi−Z¯) with S=∑i(Zi−Z¯)2. Show that it dominates Z when p≥4.

exr-shr-lambda-max.title: A1
exr-shr-lambda-max.html: Suppose maxj|xj⊤y| is attained at a single j∗. Show that for λ slightly below λmax the lasso solution has one nonzero coordinate, j∗, with the sign of xj∗⊤y and absolute value (|xj∗⊤y|−λ)/‖xj∗‖2.

exr-shr-laplace.title: B2
exr-shr-laplace.html: Let 𝛃𝛃Y∣β∼Nn(Xβ,σ2I) with σ2 known, and let the βj be independent with density (λ/2σ2)exp⁡(−λ|βj|/σ2). Show that the posterior mode is the lasso estimate. Is the posterior mean sparse?

exr-shr-lasso-df.title: C1
exr-shr-lasso-df.html: In the orthonormal case with normal errors, show that σ−2∑jCov(Sλ(β^j),β^j)=E#{j:|β^j|>λ}: the expected number of nonzero coefficients plays the role of degrees of freedom (compare @exr-shr-df-covariance). Hint: integrate by parts, one coordinate at a time.

exr-shr-no-linear-dominance.title: B1
exr-shr-no-linear-dominance.html: Let X have full column rank and let 𝛃β~=AY with AX≠I. Show that there is a 𝛃β for which 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃E‖β~−β‖2>E‖β^−β‖2. So no biased linear estimator dominates least squares.

exr-shr-orthonormal-path.title: B3
exr-shr-orthonormal-path.html: Under an orthonormal design, describe the lasso path: show that it is piecewise linear with kinks at λ=|β^j|, that variables enter in decreasing order of |β^j|, and that none ever leaves.

exr-shr-orthonormal-ridge.title: A2
exr-shr-orthonormal-ridge.html: Suppose X⊤X=I. Show that 𝛃𝛃β^λR=β^/(1+λ), df(λ)=p/(1+λ), and that the value of λ minimizing the total mean squared error is 𝛃pσ2/‖β‖2.

exr-shr-pcr-not-selection.title: A1
exr-shr-pcr-not-selection.html: Show that for k<p the estimate 𝛃β^kPC generally has no zero coordinates, so that principal component regression reduces dimension without selecting variables. When does it set the coefficient of regressor j to zero?

exr-shr-pcr-projection.title: A2
exr-shr-pcr-projection.html: Show that the fitted values of principal component regression with k components, with an unpenalized intercept, are (n−111⊤+Mk)y, that this matrix is an orthogonal projection of rank k+1, and that its leverages are 1/n+∑j≤kuij2. Why does @thm-res-deletion apply to principal component regression but not to ridge regression?

exr-shr-pcr-vs-ridge.title: B3
exr-shr-pcr-vs-ridge.html: Consider a design with two principal directions. (i) If α2=0≠α1, show that the oracle factors of @prp-shr-canonical(c) are (τ12/(1+τ12),0), that no ridge estimate attains them, and that principal component regression with k=1 exceeds the oracle’s total mean squared error by only (σ2/d12)/(1+τ12). (ii) If α12=α22>0, show that ridge with λ=σ2/α12 attains the oracle, and that every principal component regression is strictly worse.

exr-shr-pls.title: C1
exr-shr-pls.html: The first direction of partial least squares is w1∝X⊤y, the direction maximizing the sample covariance of Xw with y over unit vectors w. Show that w1∝∑jdjcjvj, and compare with the first principal direction v1. Show that the one-dimensional fit along w1 never ignores a direction j with cj≠0.

exr-shr-ridge-constrained.title: B3
exr-shr-ridge-constrained.html: Show that for every t with 𝛃0<t<‖β^‖2 (full column rank) there is exactly one λ>0 with 𝛃‖β^λR‖2=t, and that 𝛃β^λR is then the unique minimizer of ‖y−Xb‖2 subject to ‖b‖2≤t.

exr-shr-ridge-loo.title: B1
exr-shr-ridge-loo.html: Let 𝛃β^λ,(i)R be the ridge estimate computed without case i (no intercept), and hii the ith diagonal entry of Hλ. Show that 𝛃𝛃yi−x(i)⊤β^λ,(i)R=yi−x(i)⊤β^λR1−hii.

exr-shr-ridge-wide.title: C2
exr-shr-ridge-wide.html: Let p>n. Show that 𝛃β^λR=X⊤(XX⊤+λIn)−1y, which needs only an n×n inverse, and that 𝛃β^λR∈C(X⊤). What is the limit as λ→0? Chapter 28 studies this limit.

exr-shr-scalar.title: A1
exr-shr-scalar.html: Let Y¯ be the mean of n independent observations with mean μ and variance σ2. For a constant c, find the mean squared error of cY¯ as an estimator of μ. Show that it is minimized at c∗=μ2/(μ2+σ2/n) and that cY¯ beats Y¯ iff (1−c)μ2<(1+c)σ2/n. Why is c∗ not an estimator?

exr-shr-scaling.title: C1
exr-shr-scaling.html: Least squares is equivariant under rescaling: replacing X by XG−1, with G diagonal and positive, turns the estimate into 𝛃Gβ^. By rescaling one column in @exm-shr-two-regressors by 10, show that 𝛃β~f with f1=1, f2=0 is not equivariant. Why are shrinkage estimators usually applied to standardized regressors?

exr-shr-smoother-mse.title: B2
exr-shr-smoother-mse.html: A linear smoother estimates the mean vector 𝛍μ=E(Y) by SY for a fixed n×n matrix S. Show that 𝛍𝛍E‖SY−μ‖2=σ2tr(SS⊤)+‖(I−S)μ‖2 when Cov(Y)=σ2I. For the projection S=M and 𝛍μ∈C(X), recover σ2r with r=rank(X).

exr-shr-sparsity-bound.title: C2
exr-shr-sparsity-bound.html: Show that for every λ>0 there is a lasso solution with at most min(n,p) nonzero coordinates. Hint: if the active columns of a solution are linearly dependent, move along a direction in their null space that keeps the signs and the fitted vector until a coordinate hits zero.

exr-shr-sure.title: C2
exr-shr-sure.html: Let 𝛉θ^=Z+g(Z) with g satisfying the conditions of @lem-shr-stein. Show that R^=pσ2+‖g(Z)‖2+2σ2∑i∂gi∂zi(Z) is unbiased for the risk of 𝛉θ^ (Stein’s unbiased risk estimate). Compute it for James–Stein and for soft thresholding θ^i=Sλ(Zi); how could it choose λ?

exr-shr-threshold-numbers.title: A2
exr-shr-threshold-numbers.html: With an orthonormal design and 𝛃β^=(3,−0.5,1.2)⊤, compute the lasso, ridge and hard-thresholding estimates of @thm-shr-lasso-orthonormal with λ=1.

exr-shr-two-check.title: A2
exr-shr-two-check.html: In @exm-shr-two-regressors, verify the least squares total mean squared error σ2(1/d12+1/d22)=0.4103 by hand, and check the entry for “drop the second direction” using @prp-shr-canonical(a).

lem-shr-coordinate.title: Coordinate updates
lem-shr-coordinate.html:
Fix b and j with xj≠0, and let r(j)=y−∑k≠jxkbk be the partial residual.

  1. The minimizer of Lλ over bj, with the other coordinates fixed, is Sλ(xj⊤r(j))/‖xj‖2.

  2. If b is unchanged by the update of every coordinate, then b satisfies the KKT conditions @eq-shr-kkt, and is therefore a lasso solution.

lem-shr-stein.title: Stein’s lemma
lem-shr-stein.html:
1. Let Z∼N(μ,σ2), and let g:R→R be absolutely continuous with E|g′(Z)|<∞. Then E|(Z−μ)g(Z)|<∞ and E[(Z−μ)g(Z)]=σ2Eg′(Z).

  2. Let 𝛉Z∼Np(θ,σ2I), and let g=(g1,…,gp):Rp→Rp be such that, for each i and almost every value of the other coordinates, gi is absolutely continuous in zi, with E|∂gi(Z)/∂zi|<∞ and E|(Zi−θi)gi(Z)|<∞. Then 𝛉E[(Z−θ)⊤g(Z)]=σ2E∑i=1p∂gi∂zi(Z).{#eq-shr-stein}

prp-shr-canonical.title: Shrinking along the principal directions
prp-shr-canonical.html:
Let 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ, Cov(Y)=σ2I and rank(X)=p. For fixed factors fj:

  1. 𝛃𝛃E‖β~f−β‖2=∑j{fj2σ2/dj2+(1−fj)2αj2};

  2. 𝛃𝛃E‖Xβ~f−Xβ‖2=∑j{fj2σ2+(1−fj)2dj2αj2};

  3. both are minimized by the same factors fj∗=τj2/(1+τj2), and the minima are ∑j(σ2/dj2)τj2/(1+τj2) and σ2∑jτj2/(1+τj2);

  4. replacing fj=1 by some fj∈[0,1), with the other factors fixed, lowers both quantities iff τj2<(1+fj)/(1−fj). In particular dropping direction j (fj=0) helps iff τj2<1.

prp-shr-centring.title: An unpenalized intercept
prp-shr-centring.html: Let X0 be an n×p matrix of regressors with column means x¯0, let X=X0−1x¯0⊤ and y~=y−y¯1 be the centred regressors and response, and let P:Rp→[0,∞] be any function. Then (β0,b) minimizes ‖y−β01−X0b‖2+P(b) iff b minimizes ‖y~−Xb‖2+P(b) and β0=y¯−x¯0⊤b.

prp-shr-empirical-bayes.title: James–Stein as empirical Bayes
prp-shr-empirical-bayes.html:
Let 𝛉θ∼Np(0,ω2I) and 𝛉𝛉Z∣θ∼Np(θ,σ2I), p≥3, and put B=σ2/(σ2+ω2).

  1. The posterior mean is 𝛉E(θ∣Z)=(1−B)Z, and its Bayes risk is 𝛉E‖(1−B)Z−θ‖2=pσ2(1−B).

  2. Marginally Z∼Np(0,(σ2+ω2)I), and (p−2)σ2/‖Z‖2 is an unbiased estimator of B.

  3. The Bayes risk of 𝛉θ^JS is pσ2(1−B)+2σ2B.

prp-shr-lasso-path.title: Piecewise linearity
prp-shr-lasso-path.html: Suppose that for all λ in an interval [λ1,λ2] with λ1>0 the lasso solution is unique, has the same active set A={j:β^λ,jL≠0} and the same signs sA, and that XA, the columns of X in A, has full column rank. Then on that interval 𝛃β^λ,AL=(XA⊤XA)−1(XA⊤y−λsA), an affine function of λ, and the other coordinates are zero.

prp-shr-pcr.title: Bias and variance of principal component regression
prp-shr-pcr.title_html: Bias and variance of principal component regression
prp-shr-pcr.html:
Let 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ, Cov(Y)=σ2I, 𝛂𝛃α=V⊤β and τj2=dj2αj2/σ2.

  1. 𝛃β^kPC is the least squares estimate subject to the p−k restrictions vj⊤b=0, j>k. Its fitted vector is Mky, where Mk=∑j≤kujuj⊤ is the orthogonal projection onto span(z1,…,zk).

  2. 𝛃𝛃Eβ^kPC−β=−∑j>kαjvj and 𝛃Cov(β^kPC)=σ2∑j≤kdj−2vjvj⊤. The total mean squared error is ∑j>kαj2+σ2∑j≤kdj−2, and the mean squared error of the fitted values is 𝛃𝛃E‖Xβ^kPC−Xβ‖2=kσ2+∑j>kdj2αj2.

  3. 𝛃β^kPC is at least as good as 𝛃β^ in the matrix sense iff ∑j>kτj2≤1.

  4. Among all estimators 𝛃β~f with every fj∈{0,1}, both mean squared errors in

    1. are minimized by keeping exactly the directions with τj2>1 (ties may go either way). Principal component regression with k components is this best selection iff τj2≥1 for j≤k and τj2≤1 for j>k.

prp-shr-positive-part.title: Positive-part James–Stein
prp-shr-positive-part.html: In the setting of @thm-shr-james-stein, the estimator 𝛉θ^JS+=(1−(p−2)σ2‖Z‖2)+Z has strictly smaller risk than 𝛉θ^JS for every 𝛉θ.

thm-shr-bias-variance.title: Bias–variance decomposition for linear estimators
thm-shr-bias-variance.html:
1. For any estimator with finite second moments, 𝛉𝛉𝛅𝛅MSE(θ~)=Cov(θ~)+δδ⊤. For every a∈Rq, 𝛉𝛉𝛉E(a⊤θ~−a⊤θ)2=a⊤MSE(θ~)a, and for every nonnegative definite W, 𝛉𝛉𝛉𝛉𝛉E[(θ~−θ)⊤W(θ~−θ)]=tr(WMSE(θ~)).

  2. Suppose 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ and Cov(Y)=σ2I, and let 𝛃β~=AY be a linear estimator of 𝛃β. Then 𝛅𝛃δ=(AX−I)β and 𝛃𝛃𝛃MSE(β~)=σ2AA⊤+(AX−I)ββ⊤(AX−I)⊤.

  3. In the setting of (b), let X have full column rank, let 𝛃β^ be least squares, and put ΔA=σ2(X⊤X)−1−σ2AA⊤, the covariance that 𝛃β~ saves. The following are equivalent:

    1. 𝛃β~ is at least as good as 𝛃β^ in the matrix sense;

    2. 𝛃𝛃𝛃E(a⊤β~−a⊤β)2≤Var(a⊤β^) for every a;

    3. 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃E[(β~−β)⊤W(β~−β)]≤E[(β^−β)⊤W(β^−β)] for every nonnegative definite W;

    4. ΔA is nonnegative definite, 𝛅δ∈C(ΔA) and 𝛅𝛅δ⊤ΔA+δ≤1.

    When ΔA is positive definite, (iv) reads 𝛅𝛅δ⊤ΔA−1δ≤1.

thm-shr-james-stein.title: James–Stein
thm-shr-james-stein.html:
Let 𝛉Z∼Np(θ,σ2I) with p≥3 and σ2 known, and for a constant c let 𝛉θ^c=(1−cσ2/‖Z‖2)Z. Then E‖Z‖−2<∞ and:

  1. 𝛉𝛉E‖θ^c−θ‖2=pσ2−c{2(p−2)−c}σ4E‖Z‖−2. This is below pσ2 for every 𝛉θ iff 0<c<2(p−2), and smallest at c=p−2. The James–Stein estimator is 𝛉θ^JS=(1−(p−2)σ2‖Z‖2)Z, with risk 𝛉𝛉E‖θ^JS−θ‖2=pσ2−(p−2)2σ4E‖Z‖−2<pσ2.{#eq-shr-js}

  2. With 𝛉γ=‖θ‖2/σ2 and K∼Poisson(γ/2), σ2E‖Z‖−2=E{1/(p−2+2K)}. The risk of 𝛉θ^JS depends on 𝛉θ only through γ, equals 2σ2 at 𝛉θ=0, increases strictly in γ, and tends to pσ2 as γ→∞.

thm-shr-lasso-kkt.title: Lasso solutions
thm-shr-lasso-kkt.html:
Let λ>0.

  1. Lλ has at least one minimizer, and the set of minimizers is convex.

  2. b minimizes Lλ iff it satisfies the KKT conditions @eq-shr-kkt.

  3. All minimizers have the same fitted vector Xb and the same norm ‖b‖1. If X has full column rank, the minimizer is unique.

  4. 0 is a minimizer iff λ≥λmax=‖X⊤y‖∞=maxj|xj⊤y|.

  5. Every minimizer b^ also minimizes ‖y−Xb‖2 subject to ‖b‖1≤‖b^‖1.

thm-shr-lasso-orthonormal.title: Three kinds of shrinkage under an orthonormal design
thm-shr-lasso-orthonormal.title_html: Three kinds of shrinkage under an orthonormal design
thm-shr-lasso-orthonormal.html:
Suppose X⊤X=I, so that 𝛃β^=X⊤y, and let λ>0.

  1. (Lasso.) The unique minimizer of @eq-shr-lasso is given by β^λ,jL=Sλ(β^j).

  2. (Ridge.) The minimizer of @eq-shr-ridge-criterion is 𝛃β^/(1+λ).

  3. (Subset selection.) The minimizers of 12‖y−Xb‖2+12λ2#{j:bj≠0} are given by bj=Hλ(β^j) (with either choice when |β^j|=λ), and for each k the best subset of size k consists of the k largest |β^j|.

thm-shr-ridge.title: Ridge regression
thm-shr-ridge.html:
Let λ>0.

  1. (Closed form.) The criterion @eq-shr-ridge-criterion has the unique minimizer 𝛃β^λR=(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y=∑j≤rdjdj2+λcjvj. If r=p, then 𝛃β^λR=∑jfj(λ)α^jvj with shrinkage factors fj(λ)=dj2/(dj2+λ)∈(0,1), decreasing in λ and smallest for the smallest dj.

  2. (Fitted values.) 𝛃Xβ^λR=Hλy with Hλ=X(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤=∑j≤rfj(λ)ujuj⊤. The effective degrees of freedom df(λ)=trHλ=∑j≤rfj(λ) decrease strictly from r (as λ→0) to 0 (as λ→∞).

  3. (Moments.) If 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ, Cov(Y)=σ2I and r=p, then 𝛃𝛃𝛃Eβ^λR−β=−λ(X⊤X+λI)−1β, 𝛃Cov(β^λR)=σ2∑jdj2(dj2+λ)2vjvj⊤, and, with 𝛂𝛃α=V⊤β, the total mean squared error is 𝛃𝛃E‖β^λR−β‖2=σ2∑jdj2(dj2+λ)2+λ2∑jαj2(dj2+λ)2.{#eq-shr-ridge-mse}

  4. (The path.) Unless X⊤y=0, 𝛃‖β^λR‖ decreases strictly in λ, with limit 0 as λ→∞; and 𝛃β^λR→X+y, the least squares estimate of smallest norm, as λ→0.

  5. (Bayesian reading.) If 𝛃𝛃Y∣β∼Nn(Xβ,σ2I) with σ2 known and 𝛃β∼Np(0,(σ2/λ)I), then 𝛃𝛃β∣Y∼Np(β^λR,σ2(X⊤X+λI)−1). With σ2 unknown and the normal–inverse-gamma prior of @thm-opt-bayes-conjugate with m0=0 and V0=λ−1I, the posterior mean of 𝛃β is again 𝛃β^λR.

thm-shr-ridge-dominates.title: Hoerl–Kennard
thm-shr-ridge-dominates.html:
Let X have full column rank, 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ, Cov(Y)=σ2I with σ2>0, and let αmax2=maxjαj2 with 𝛂𝛃α=V⊤β. Let m(λ) be the total mean squared error @eq-shr-ridge-mse, so that m(0)=σ2∑jdj−2 is that of least squares.

  1. m(λ)<m(0) for every 0<λ<2σ2/αmax2, and in particular for every 𝛃0<λ<2σ2/‖β‖2. If 𝛃β=0, for every λ>0.

  2. m is strictly decreasing on [0,σ2/αmax2].

  3. 𝛃β^λR is at least as good as 𝛃β^ in the matrix sense iff λσ2∑jdj2αj22dj2+λ≤1, which holds whenever 𝛃0<λ≤2σ2/‖β‖2.
